summary: Defines the two metering and marking behaviors of PCN nodes, which protect the quality of service of inelastic flows in a Diffserv domain. Threshold metering marks packets once a load level is passed, with a second behavior as well.

plainLanguage.summary:
Some traffic, such as live video, cannot slow down when a network gets busy. PCN watches how much of that traffic passes each link and marks packets once the rate passes a limit set below the link's capacity, so the edges of the network can act before the network congests.

This RFC defines the two ways a node can meter that traffic and mark the packets.

questions: what is pcn excess traffic marking
how does pcn admission control work
subtitle: How a network node warns the edges of a domain that its traffic is approaching the limit.

tldr.problem: Traffic such as live media cannot slow down when a network gets busy, so a domain needs to know that it is running out of room before the queues build up.
tldr.mechanism: Every link meters the PCN traffic on it with two token buckets. One marks all PCN packets once the rate passes a threshold; the other marks only the packets that are above a higher rate.
tldr.outcome: The marked packets tell the boundary nodes of the domain whether to admit a new flow or to terminate an existing one. The document is a Proposed Standard and depends on the PCN architecture in RFC 5559.

facts.label: The meters work on
facts.value: All PCN packets on a link, not on individual flows

facts.label: Threshold meter rule
facts.value: Mark when the bucket fill is below the threshold

today: RFC 5670 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It defines the metering and marking behaviours of PCN nodes, and depends on the PCN architecture in RFC 5559 and on the baseline encoding in RFC 5696. The example algorithms and the implementation notes are informative appendices.

sections.title: Early Warning Before Congestion
sections.content:
Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) exists to protect the quality of service of inelastic flows inside a Diffserv domain, in a way that is simple, scalable and robust. Inelastic flows are the ones that cannot slow down when the network is busy, such as live media.

Two mechanisms do the protecting. Admission control decides whether to admit a new flow or block it. Flow termination decides, in abnormal circumstances, whether to terminate some of the flows that are already running. Both rely on the same measurement: on every link in the domain the overall rate of PCN traffic is metered, and packets are marked when configured rates are exceeded. Those rates sit below the rate of the link, so the boundary nodes hear about an overload before any congestion happens. That is where the name comes from.

The level of marking lets the boundary nodes decide whether to admit or to terminate. Inside the domain, PCN traffic is forwarded in a prioritised Diffserv traffic class.

This document defines the two metering and marking behaviours of PCN nodes. Their aim is to give an early warning of potential congestion before there is any significant build-up of PCN packets in the queues. The two behaviours are:

  • Threshold-metering and -marking: mark all PCN packets, with a threshold-mark, when the bit rate of PCN traffic is greater than its configured reference rate, the PCN-threshold-rate.
  • Excess-traffic-metering and -marking: when the bit rate of PCN packets is greater than its configured reference rate, the PCN-excess-rate, mark PCN packets with an excess-traffic-mark at a rate equal to the difference between the rate of PCN traffic and the PCN-excess-rate.

RFC 3168 defines a broadly RED-like default congestion marking behaviour for Explicit Congestion Notification, but it allows alternatives to be defined. This document defines such an alternative. The general architecture for PCN is described in RFC 5559.
sections.plainLanguage: Some traffic, such as live video, cannot slow down when a network gets busy. PCN watches how much of that traffic passes each link and marks packets once the rate passes a limit set below the link's capacity, so the edges of the network can act before the network congests.

sections.title: Competing Non-PCN Traffic and Metered Packets
sections.content:
Two terms do most of the work in this document.

  • A competing-non-PCN-packet is a non-PCN packet that shares a link with PCN packets and competes with them for the forwarding bandwidth of that link. Competing-non-PCN-packets MUST NOT be PCN-marked, because only PCN packets can be PCN-marked. The RFC notes that in general it is not advised to have any competing-non-PCN traffic. It also notes that there is likely to be traffic, such as best effort traffic, that is forwarded at a lower priority than PCN traffic; although it shares the link, it does not compete for forwarding bandwidth, so it is not competing-non-PCN traffic.
  • A metered-packet is a packet that the metering functions measure. A PCN packet MUST be treated as a metered packet, with one minor exception noted later. A competing-non-PCN-packet MAY be treated as a metered packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic that is not PCN traffic can still share a link and take bandwidth from it. The rules call that competing traffic, and it may be measured but it must never be marked.

sections.title: Recognising PCN Traffic
sections.content:
A PCN node MUST classify a packet as a PCN packet if the value of its Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) and Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) fields corresponds to a PCN-enabled codepoint, as defined in the encoding scheme that applies to the PCN domain. RFC 5696 defines the baseline encoding. Otherwise the packet MUST NOT be classified as a PCN packet.

A PCN node MUST classify a packet as a competing-non-PCN packet if it is not a PCN packet and it competes with PCN packets for the forwarding bandwidth on a link.
sections.plainLanguage: The node recognises PCN traffic by looking at the two fields that carry a packet's service class and its congestion state. A packet that matches the configured code point is PCN traffic; anything else that competes for the link is competing traffic.

sections.title: Dropping Packets When a Link Is Overloaded
sections.content:
If the queue of a PCN node overflows, packets are dropped anyway. This section describes the extra action that may be taken.

On all links in the PCN domain, dropping MAY be done by first metering all metered packets to see whether the rate of metered traffic on the link is greater than the rate allowed for such traffic, and dropping metered packets if it is too high.

If the node does drop PCN packets, two rules apply. PCN packets that arrive at the node already excess-traffic-marked SHOULD be dropped first. And the node's excess-traffic-meter SHOULD NOT meter the PCN packets that it drops, which in practice means doing the dropping before the metering.
sections.plainLanguage: Dropping is optional and only for when a link is genuinely overloaded. If packets are dropped, the ones already marked as excess traffic go first, and dropped packets are not counted by the meter.

sections.title: The Threshold Meter
sections.content:
A PCN node MUST implement a threshold-meter whose behaviour is functionally equivalent to the following.

The meter acts like a token bucket sized in bits, with a configured reference rate in bits per second. The amount of tokens in the bucket is called F_tm. Tokens are added at the reference rate, the PCN-threshold-rate, up to a maximum of BS_tm, and are removed in the amount equal to the size in bits of each metered packet, down to a minimum of F_tm = 0. The letters stand for fill of the token bucket, bucket size, and threshold-meter.

The bucket has a configured intermediate depth called the threshold. If F_tm is below the threshold, the meter tells the marking function that the packet is to be threshold-marked. Otherwise it does not.

Appendix B adds that the reference rate of the threshold meter is configured at less than the rate allocated to the PCN traffic class, and is less than or possibly equal to the PCN-excess-rate. It also notes that all PCN packets, even if they are already marked, are metered by the threshold meter, unlike the excess-traffic meter, because every packet should contribute to the decision about whether there is room for a new flow.
sections.plainLanguage: The threshold meter is a token bucket that fills at a set rate and empties as packets pass. When the amount left in the bucket drops below the configured threshold, the packet is marked. Every PCN packet is measured, marked or not.

sections.title: The Excess-Traffic Meter
sections.content:
A packet SHOULD NOT be metered by the excess-traffic meter in two cases: when the PCN packet is already excess-traffic-marked on arrival, and when the node drops the packet. Otherwise the PCN packet MUST be treated as a metered packet.

A PCN node MUST implement an excess-traffic-meter. It SHOULD indicate packets to be excess-traffic-marked independently of their size. If that packet size independent marking is not implemented, the meter MUST use the classic metering behaviour instead.

Both behaviours use a token bucket sized in bits with a configured reference rate, the PCN-excess-rate. Tokens are added at that rate up to a maximum of BS_etm, and the amount in the bucket is called F_etm. In the classic behaviour, tokens are removed equal to the size in bits of the metered packet, down to a minimum of F_etm = 0, and if the bucket is empty when a packet arrives the meter says the packet is to be excess-traffic-marked. In the packet size independent behaviour, tokens are removed only while the bucket is not negative, and a packet is marked when the bucket is negative, in which case no tokens are removed.

Appendix B explains why the packet size independent version is preferred: with the classic behaviour, large packets are more likely to be marked than small ones, so with some edge behaviours flows with large packets are more likely to be terminated. With packet size independent marking, either the packet is marked or tokens are removed, never both, so the token bucket cannot become more negative than the maximum packet size on the link.
sections.plainLanguage: The second meter marks only the traffic that is above the configured rate. It is meant to treat packets of all sizes the same way, so that a flow sending large packets is not singled out for termination.

sections.title: Marking the Packet
sections.content:
A PCN packet MUST be marked to reflect the metering results by setting its encoding state appropriately, as specified by the encoding scheme that applies in the PCN domain. A consistent choice of encoding scheme MUST be made throughout a PCN domain.

A PCN node MUST NOT PCN-mark a packet that is not a PCN packet, MUST NOT change a non-PCN packet into a PCN packet, and MUST NOT change a PCN packet into a non-PCN packet. Competing-non-PCN packets MAY be metered, but they MUST NOT be PCN-marked.

Appendix B notes what these rules forbid in practice. A node is not allowed to downgrade a PCN packet into a lower priority Diffserv behaviour aggregate, so downgrading is not an alternative to dropping. And where competing traffic is metered, the meter may say a packet should be marked while the marking function knows that it cannot be; what to do then is left to the implementation, and one simple possibility is to mark the next PCN packet instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The mark is written into the packet by changing its encoding state, using the scheme chosen for that domain. A node must not mark traffic that is not PCN traffic, and must not turn PCN traffic into ordinary traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document assumes that all PCN nodes are PCN-enabled and are trusted to meter and mark truthfully. If that is not the case there are numerous potential attacks. A rogue PCN interior node could PCN-mark all packets, so that no flows were admitted, or it could mark no packets even when it is pre-congested.

The RFC notes that PCN interior nodes are not flow-aware, and that this prevents some attacks in which an attacker targets specific flows in the data plane, for instance for denial of service or eavesdropping.

On security operations and management, PCN adds few specifics to the general good practice required in this field, as set out in RFC 4778. One example is that it may be sensible for a PCN node to raise an alarm if it is persistently PCN-marking. Security considerations are further discussed in RFC 5559.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme trusts every node in the domain to report congestion honestly. A node that lied could block all traffic or hide a real overload, so the trust has to be justified by the network operator.

items.text: A PCN packet must not be changed back into a non-PCN packet.
